name: Anastrozole
lead: Anastrozole, sold as Arimidex among other names, is a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor taken by mouth. Its approved uses are in postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, where it lowers oestrogen by blocking the aromatase enzyme.[1][2] It is a prescription medicine.

In bodybuilding and testosterone-therapy settings it is used to manage oestrogen, and on looksmax.org it is discussed by users, including self-described teenagers, who hope to delay growth-plate closure and increase adult height, often alongside growth hormone.[3][4][5] Published research on aromatase inhibitors for height or for gynecomastia in healthy males is limited; a 2023 review of gynecomastia in boys says anastrozole and letrozole have not been consistently useful in that age group.[6]

Documented adverse effects from the US label include reduced bone mineral density, raised cholesterol and ischaemic cardiovascular events in women with prior heart disease, and possible fetal harm.[7] Looksmaxxing use for height is off-label and, for adolescents, is not an approved indication.
infobox: Hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women

paras: The US label lists adjuvant treatment of hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer in postmenopausal women, first-line treatment of locally advanced or metastatic disease, and treatment of advanced disease progressing after tamoxifen.[7] The ATAC trial and other randomised trials compared anastrozole with tamoxifen in this setting,[8][9][10] and a 2010 review summarises its pharmacology and comparative efficacy and safety against tamoxifen.[11] Grokipedia also describes off-label use in breast-cancer prevention and in precocious puberty in boys, based on small studies and case series.[1]

Appearance-related interest centres on three ideas: increasing height by delaying skeletal maturation, controlling oestrogen-related effects such as gynecomastia or water retention while using testosterone, and, on looksmax.org, improving body composition.[3][4][12] The 2023 review of gynecomastia in boys states that tamoxifen has been tried successfully in adolescents while anastrozole and letrozole have not been consistently useful.[6]

Label warnings include increased ischaemic cardiovascular events compared with tamoxifen in women with pre-existing ischaemic heart disease, decreases in bone mineral density, increased total cholesterol, and embryo-fetal toxicity.[7] A review of the drug's safety profile reports similar themes in postmenopausal women.[11] Forum participants themselves raise concerns about crashing oestrogen, with one stating that without exogenous testosterone the result is lowered oestrogen and bone loss, and another reporting that long-term use makes a person lazy and slow.[3][12]

Oestrogen drives epiphyseal fusion in both sexes, a point forum users cite in explaining why aromatase inhibitors are discussed for height; the same hormone also supports bone density, which is why label warnings about bone loss are relevant to people considering use in adolescence. Published trials in healthy adolescents were not identified.

Anastrozole is a selective non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor. The aromatase enzyme converts androgens (androstenedione and testosterone) to oestrone and oestradiol, and anastrozole's inhibition of it significantly lowers serum oestradiol.[7] Forum users contrast it with the steroidal inhibitor exemestane, saying anastrozole crosses the blood-brain barrier less and has fewer androgenic effects.[13]

The evidence base is overwhelmingly in breast cancer: the ATAC trial (anastrozole versus tamoxifen, alone or combined),[8][9][10] a North American first-line trial,[14] and ongoing combination trials with CDK4/6 inhibitors.[15][16][17] Registered studies include bioavailability studies in healthy volunteers, a gynecomastia extension study, a trial in McCune-Albright syndrome and a trial in elderly hypogonadal men.[18][19][20]
No published randomised trial in healthy adolescents testing anastrozole to increase adult height was identified in the sources reviewed.

Many looksmax.org threads, several started by people who describe themselves as 13 to 16 years old, ask which aromatase inhibitor to use for height, how it pairs with growth hormone or MK-677, and where to obtain it without a prescription.[4][5][13][21][22] Some replies caution against it: one answers that they would not use an aromatase inhibitor in the first place, and a thread titled with a warning advises against aromatase inhibitors outright.[3][23] Other posters say it should be used only with bloodwork guidance, typically alongside exogenous testosterone.[12] On T Nation, users on testosterone replacement discuss adding anastrozole to manage oestradiol, and some report fatigue or other effects they attribute to it or to hCG.[24][25]

timeline.event: First results of the ATAC randomised trial of anastrozole versus tamoxifen published.[8]

lore.intro: Anastrozole is discussed mostly as a heightmaxxing and oestrogen-control drug, frequently by teenagers, and users debate it against exemestane and letrozole.[3][4][13]

claims.claim: Anastrozole delays growth-plate closure and increases adult height
claims.believers: Posters recommend it, often with growth hormone, to extend the growth window by reducing oestrogen.[3][4]
claims.experts: Controlled evidence in healthy adolescents was not found; a review of gynecomastia in boys says aromatase inhibitors have not been consistently useful there, and trial evidence in precocious puberty is limited to small studies.[6]

claims.claim: Taken alone, anastrozole crashes oestrogen and bone mass
claims.believers: An experienced poster says that without exogenous testosterone, oestrogen is simply crashed and bone mass destroyed.[12]
claims.experts: The label warns of decreased bone mineral density.[7]

claims.claim: Anastrozole is better than exemestane for heightmaxxing because it has fewer androgenic effects
claims.believers: A reply states a non-steroidal inhibitor always wins in this scenario.[13]
claims.experts: No comparative trials in this use were found.

claims.claim: Long-term use causes lethargy and mental slowness
claims.believers: A user says long-term use makes you lazy and slow, comparing it to cannabis.[3]
claims.experts: Fatigue appears among adverse effects discussed in clinical use, but no controlled data on this claim in healthy adolescents were found.[11]

card.summary: A breast-cancer aromatase inhibitor that teen heightmaxxers and TRT users discuss for oestrogen control; no trials show a height gain in healthy people.
card.note: Label warns of bone loss and cardiovascular events; off-label use for height in adolescents is untested.

quick.overview:
Anastrozole (Arimidex) is a prescription aromatase inhibitor for breast cancer in postmenopausal women. In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed for delaying growth-plate closure to gain height, and for oestrogen control during testosterone use.

No controlled trial shows it increases height in healthy adolescents; a gynecomastia review says it has not been consistently useful in boys.
quick.mechanism: It blocks aromatase, the enzyme converting testosterone and androstenedione to oestrogen, lowering oestradiol. Oestrogen drives growth-plate fusion, which is the basis of height-related interest.
quick.risks: The label lists reduced bone density, higher cholesterol, cardiovascular events in women with heart disease and fetal harm. Forum users report fatigue and crashed oestrogen. Prescription-only; its use for height is off-label.
